routes.description: Establish that agency and rational normativity cannot be reduced to causal compulsion, then use Bradleyan idealism to place lawful explanation within a wider experiential reality.
routes.successCriteria: Show that determinist inference does not eliminate agential sourcehood or relevant modal alternatives and that idealism integrates domains that reductive naturalism leaves unexplained.

motionBridge.description: Libertarian idealism must preserve meaningful agency under lawful description while providing a more comprehensive account of experience than naturalistic reduction.

centralBridges.description: Distinguish mathematical or logical determination from causal compulsion and explain why the former need not displace agents as sources.
Supply an account of alternative possibility and sourcehood that does not depend upon a presently branching physical timeline.
Show why scientific representation is one mode within experience rather than an exhaustive inventory of reality.
Explain how truth, value, feeling, and inquiry can be integrated without reducing them to abstract thought alone.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Connect indispensable responsibility practices to a real distinction between agency and mere bodily occurrence.
Identify experiential, practical, and intellectual constraints that prevent idealism from collapsing into arbitrary invention.

routes.description: Maintain determinist pressure on libertarian alternatives while reconstructing freedom and inquiry through their practical functions without requiring Bradleyan metaphysics.
routes.successCriteria: Show that changing causal vocabulary or modal scope does not secure libertarian freedom, and that pragmatic standards preserve responsibility and disciplined inquiry more economically.

motionBridge.description: Compatibilist pragmatism must retain action-guiding freedom and standards of inquiry while showing that libertarian idealism adds no necessary explanatory gain.

centralBridges.description: Establish that fixed laws and states threaten genuine alternatives even when the determining relation is described as non-causal.
Test whether varying pasts or laws answers the fixed-premise consequence challenge or merely changes the relevant possible worlds.
Explain freedom through the practical distinctions needed for incentives, responsibility, praise, and blame under determinism.
Provide disciplined pragmatic standards for experience-centered inquiry without committing to a substantially existent absolute.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish perspectival or mind-framed access to reality from voluntary construction or mind-controlled truth.
Retain methodological pluralism while specifying constraints that exclude both scientistic reduction and unrestricted inclusion.

sections.title: Determinism, causation, and agential sourcehood
sections.rationale: This issue contains the motion's primary clash over whether complete lawful determination amounts to causal constraint and whether agency can remain explanatorily fundamental.

sections.title: Alternative possibilities and the consequence argument
sections.rationale: The modal scope of doing otherwise determines whether libertarian freedom survives a fixed timeline and whether sourcehood can be separated from control over past facts and laws.

sections.title: Practical responsibility and metaphysical agency
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether freedom's indispensable social functions are sufficient for compatibilism or instead presuppose a deeper distinction between genuine action and bodily occurrence.

sections.title: Experience, science, and naturalistic reduction
sections.rationale: The comparative metaphysical burden turns on whether science exhausts reality, whether other experiential domains require systematic inclusion, and whether a restrained naturalistic idealism can include experience.

sections.title: The absolute and the completion of inquiry
sections.rationale: This issue addresses whether Bradleyan integration names a real completion that grounds inquiry or only an aspirational ideal whose substantial existence remains unestablished.

moves.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
moves.proposition: Agency is needed to make sense of practical life, while objections to libertarian agency rely on contestable physicalist and causal-closure assumptions.
moves.attributionBasis: Folley directly asks Hawkins about his libertarian position, and the uninterrupted answer is delivered in Hawkins's first-person voice.

response.rationale: As an opening constructive, the move establishes the practical indispensability of agency and cautiously distinguishes that claim from a full defense of libertarianism.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The opening clearly motivates an agency burden, but its attack on physicalism and causal closure remains compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The practical-agency thesis and its compatibility qualification are recoverable, though the relevant stronger sense of agency is not yet fully specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move expressly concedes that compatibilism supplies much of the practical account and advances only a qualified further claim.

charity.alternative: Compatibilism may preserve the practical agency needed for everyday and moral life without libertarian sourcehood.
charity.decisiveQualification: The speaker explicitly grants that compatibilism provides most of what practical life requires before claiming that something further remains.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The practical-indispensability inference is coherent, with one unresolved bridge from agency generally to libertarian agency.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Practical-life considerations support an agency concept, but the physicalism and closure objections are principally asserted here.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly advances the subsidiary practice bridge, although it does not yet complete the libertarian inference.

representationalCharity.rationale: The live compatibilist alternative is presented in a strong form and expressly conceded substantial explanatory value.

moves.evidenceBasis: The locked proposition and excerpt expressly appeal to everyday and philosophical practice, concede compatibilism's reach, and reserve a further free-will claim.

moves.speaker: Joe Folley
moves.proposition: Complete knowledge of particle states and natural laws appears sufficient to derive every later event, excluding genuine alternatives.
moves.attributionBasis: The host explicitly frames his naturalist audience's inherited determinist argument and then asks Hawkins where that reasoning fails.

components.text: Whether contestable physicalist assumptions are actually needed for determinist pressure against alternatives.
Whether practical reliance on agency establishes the stronger libertarian conception of agency.

response.rationale: The Laplacean derivability challenge directly supplies determinist pressure against genuine alternatives, but it does not answer the separate practical-indispensability premise.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive metaphysical challenge with a clear test case while leaving the practical premise unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conditional setup, assumed complete state-and-law knowledge, derivability claim, and target of genuine alternatives are all clear.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The argument is posed as a conditional challenge rather than as an unqualified proof that actual physics is deterministic.

charity.alternative: Agency might remain meaningful even if later events are derivable, because derivability need not be causal compulsion.
charity.decisiveQualification: The move asks where the determinist inference fails rather than assuming that derivability and causal compulsion are definitionally identical.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conditional route is intelligible, but the bridge from perfect derivability to exclusion of relevant alternatives needs defense.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The Laplacean case is appropriate support for the challenge, though actual law completeness and the modal inference remain hypothetical.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It squarely advances the central determination bridge by formulating the fixed-laws-and-state threat.

representationalCharity.rationale: The question leaves space for the strongest non-causal response, though it initially compresses the derivability-to-no-alternatives warrant.

moves.evidenceBasis: The locked excerpt specifies complete particle positions and natural laws, inferred derivability of subsequent events, and the question whether doing otherwise is ruled out.

moves.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
moves.proposition: Mathematical determination in theoretical physics is non-causal, whereas experimental causation is intervention-based and rooted in an agential perspective.
moves.attributionBasis: After Folley asks which concepts of causation support determinism, Hawkins explicitly invokes his idealist approach and delivers the extended answer.

components.text: Whether complete mathematical derivability constitutes causal determination that removes agential sourcehood.
Whether complete derivability excludes genuine modal alternatives even if the relation is non-causal.

response.rationale: The reply directly distinguishes truth-functional determination from intervention-based causation, but it does not yet show that fixed determination preserves doing otherwise.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It strongly contacts the causal premise while leaving the separate modal-exclusion component unresolved.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between theoretical mathematical relations and experimental intervention-based causation is clearly and consistently stated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The disciplinary distinction is plausible, but the move speaks strongly without fully establishing that intervention exhausts scientifically relevant causation.

charity.alternative: The determinist challenge can concern fixed dependence and excluded alternatives without claiming that the dependence is interventionist causation.
charity.decisiveQualification: Calling mathematical determination non-causal defeats only a causal-compulsion formulation unless sourcehood or modal alternatives are separately preserved.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conceptual distinction is coherent, with a remaining bridge from interventionist causation to agential sourcehood.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Experimental controls aptly illustrate intervention, but the general conclusion about causation and agency remains underdefended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supplies the pro route's central distinction between mathematical determination and causal compulsion.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly isolates a real ambiguity, but it temporarily treats that ambiguity as more damaging to the determinist challenge than it is.

moves.evidenceBasis: The locked proposition and excerpt contrast truth-functional relations in theoretical physics with experimental manipulation, controls, and an agential perspective.

moves.speaker: Joe Folley
moves.proposition: Even non-causal determination threatens libertarian freedom when fixed laws and states exclude genuinely branching alternative futures.
moves.attributionBasis: The host addresses Hawkins's preceding distinction, articulates a determinist audience's objection, and ends by posing two alternatives to Hawkins.

components.text: Whether labeling determination non-causal is sufficient to preserve libertarian alternatives under fixed laws and states.
Whether intervention-based experimental causation depends on an agential perspective.

response.rationale: The reply directly argues that predictability and a single fixed future threaten branching alternatives regardless of causal vocabulary, while leaving interventionism largely untouched.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It reaches the decisive modal consequence of the distinction, though it does not engage every claim about experimental causation.

precisionFindings.rationale: Fixed laws, fixed states, perfect prediction, and the branching-future target are identifiable and scoped to the libertarian picture under discussion.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move presents the fixed-future consequence as a serious apparent threat rather than claiming that every libertarian theory requires literal branching.

charity.alternative: Non-causal determination may coexist with agency if sourcehood does not require an open branching future.
charity.decisiveQualification: The reply targets the branching-alternatives component and does not claim that non-causal dependence by itself eliminates every possible sourcehood theory.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from fixed complete conditions to no branching future is stable, subject to the later dispute over the relevant modal scope.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The fixed-state conditional supports the objection, but perfect prediction is assumed rather than independently demonstrated.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the pro central-agency bridge by showing why a terminological causal distinction may not preserve freedom.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection accurately narrows its target, although its imagery risks associating libertarianism too closely with one branching model.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly holds states fixed, invokes perfect prediction in both temporal directions, and argues that non-causal determination still undermines branching alternatives.

moves.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
moves.proposition: Libertarian freedom need not require a presently branching timeline because sourcehood and the modal possibility of doing otherwise are separable ingredients.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly introduces his own libertarian position after contrasting it with branching-futures accounts, identifying the passage as Hawkins's answer.

components.text: Whether libertarian freedom requires a presently branching future that fixed determination would eliminate.
How sourcehood and doing otherwise can each survive under the proposed nonbranching account.

response.rationale: The reply directly rejects branching futures as necessary and separates sourcehood from alternative possibility, but the excerpt only introduces rather than completes both accounts.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive assumption but leaves the positive modal and sourcehood mechanisms materially compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The two-component theory is recoverable, though sourcehood and could-have-done-otherwise are introduced without fully stable criteria in this span.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker carefully claims that branching is not necessarily required and presents separation of ingredients as his position.

charity.alternative: Fixed laws and states may still remove the only alternatives relevant to libertarian freedom, even if broader possible worlds differ.
charity.decisiveQualification: Separating sourcehood from alternatives does not by itself show that either component survives the fixed-premise challenge.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The decomposition is coherent, but separation of concepts alone does not establish their joint satisfaction.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The proposal is philosophically relevant but receives limited positive warrant within the selected span.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central modality bridge by denying that present physical branching is necessary.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply does not caricature the branching objection, but it initially answers it at a more schematic level than its strongest formulation requires.

moves.evidenceBasis: The locked excerpt explicitly disclaims the necessity of branching futures and identifies sourcehood and could-have-done-otherwise as distinct ingredients.

moves.speaker: Joe Folley
moves.proposition: Allowing different pasts or laws changes the fixed premise rather than showing a different outcome with the actual past and laws held fixed.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage is framed as a critical question and is immediately followed by Hawkins's marked explanatory answer, matching Folley's role in the dialogue.

components.text: Whether alternatives with different past facts or laws answer the challenge when the actual past and laws are fixed.
Whether agential sourcehood can be established independently of the alternative-possibilities condition.

response.rationale: The reply directly exposes the shift from fixed P to a different P when assessing Q, but it does not independently challenge the proposed sourcehood component.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It sharply contacts the decisive modal-scope issue while leaving the separate sourcehood ingredient unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: P, Q, the fixed facts and laws, and the rival counterfactual scope are expressly identified despite conversational hesitation.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move poses a precise objection as a question and openly marks residual uncertainty rather than claiming a completed refutation.

charity.alternative: Doing otherwise may quantify over worlds with different histories or laws rather than worlds sharing the actual fixed premise.
charity.decisiveQualification: That broader modal claim does not answer the narrower consequence argument unless its relevance to actual-source control is justified.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The scope objection is clear and valid: varying P does not by itself demonstrate a different Q conditional on fixed P.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The explicit P-and-Q reconstruction strongly supports the criticism, with the normative relevance of fixed-P possibility still contestable.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It almost exactly states the central consequence bridge's required test.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply states the broader-world interpretation accurately before identifying the exact unresolved fixed-premise qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt defines P as past facts and laws, Q as the decision, and contrasts holding P fixed with claiming that a different P would yield a different Q.

moves.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
moves.proposition: The consequence argument conflates logical dependence with agential dependence when it transfers lack of control over past facts into lack of control over present acts.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage directly answers Folley's question, develops Hawkins's first-person idealist account of agency, and ends before Folley's next marked intervention.

components.text: Whether lack of control over fixed past facts validly transfers through logical dependence to lack of sourcehood over present action.
Whether a different outcome is possible while the actual past and laws remain fixed.

response.rationale: The reply expressly diagnoses the transfer from logical implication to agential dependence as invalid, thereby challenging why the original fixed-P demand should govern sourcehood.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It gives a clear defect and defeating consequence, though it does not separately establish same-P alternative possibility.

precisionFindings.rationale: Logical connection, sourcehood, control over P, and control over Q are clearly distinguished, with one caveat about relevant dependence left implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The alleged conflation is well identified, but some consequence arguments invoke modal transfer principles rather than simple causal or source transfer.

charity.alternative: The consequence argument can rely on a modal no-choice transfer principle, not on the claim that logical implication literally transmits causal sourcehood.
charity.decisiveQualification: The move is decisive against an unargued sourcehood transfer but not automatically against every defended modal transfer rule.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between logical dependence and agential dependence is coherent and directly undermines an unsupported transfer.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual diagnosis is supported, but the broader claim that this mistake pervades the consequence argument needs comparison with stronger formulations.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the con consequence bridge at its transfer inference.

representationalCharity.rationale: The criticism identifies a genuine weakness but represents the strongest consequence argument too narrowly as a common logical-to-agential conflation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly denies that control or sourcehood must follow mathematical implication from P to Q and identifies the transfer as a recurring philosophical mistake.

moves.speaker: Joe Folley
moves.proposition: The competing accounts may quantify over different possible worlds, leaving the fixed-past challenge unresolved rather than substantively rebutted.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage follows Hawkins's extended answer as a skeptical reformulation and is followed by Hawkins's marked response, clearly identifying Folley as speaker.

components.text: Whether the dispute concerns different modal scopes rather than a direct refutation of the fixed-past challenge.
Whether logical dependence licenses transfer of lack of sourcehood from past facts to present action.
Whether broader possible-world alternatives satisfy the libertarian could-have-done-otherwise condition.

response.rationale: The reply clarifies that the parties quantify over different sets of worlds, preserving the fixed-past question, but it does not answer the specific logical-to-agential transfer criticism.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It effectively reframes the scope dispute while leaving the most recent transfer objection materially unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The two quantificational scopes and the condition of keeping past and laws fixed are stated explicitly and without material ambiguity.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move expressly allows that the broader quantification is legitimate while explaining why it does not settle the narrower question.

charity.alternative: The pro account legitimately evaluates alternatives across worlds where past or laws vary.
charity.decisiveQualification: Legitimacy of that modal scope does not show that it answers the distinct fixed-past consequence challenge.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The differing-scope diagnosis follows cleanly and avoids treating either quantificational choice as internally illegitimate.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The possible-world comparison adequately supports the diagnosis, though it does not defend why fixed-past scope is normatively privileged.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly advances the central consequence bridge by isolating the surviving fixed-premise issue.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply states the opposing scope as legitimate and identifies disagreement without replacing it with a weaker view.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts worlds in which past and future may vary with worlds restricted by fixed past facts and laws, while expressly calling the former scope legitimate.

moves.speaker: Joe Folley
moves.proposition: A pragmatically indispensable notion of freedom survives complete determinism because societies must distinguish conduct that incentives can influence from conduct they cannot.
moves.attributionBasis: The sustained first-person account follows Hawkins's response, names Folley's compatibilism, and belongs to Folley's clearly marked conversational turn.

response.rationale: As a constructive, the move supplies a concrete functional distinction—responsiveness to incentives—that can organize freedom-related practices even under determinism.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It strongly advances its constructive burden with a usable social distinction, though the account remains intentionally minimal.

precisionFindings.rationale: The deterministic setting, minimal freedom concept, and distinction between incentive-responsive and nonresponsive conduct are clearly scoped.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The necessity claim concerns society's practical sorting requirement, not the necessity of a unique metaphysical analysis, and the conception is labeled minimal.

charity.alternative: Libertarian sourcehood may explain why responsibility practices are justified rather than merely socially useful.
charity.decisiveQualification: The move claims that a functional distinction survives determinism, not that this alone settles every question about desert or ultimate sourcehood.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from unavoidable incentive practices to a minimal functional distinction is clear and internally consistent.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The social example is compelling support, although empirical and normative details about incentives remain compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies the central functional bridge for compatibilist pragmatism.

representationalCharity.rationale: The constructive does not directly represent libertarianism, but its limited functional claim avoids displacing the stronger rival by stipulation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The locked excerpt places the case in a fully deterministic society and distinguishes behavior appropriately affected by incentives from behavior that is not.

moves.speaker: Joe Folley
moves.proposition: Freedom should be analyzed through the functions of praise, blame, and incentives rather than assumed to possess a single metaphysical essence.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted turn continues Folley's first-person examples and explicitly develops the compatibilist analysis introduced earlier in his speech.

response.rationale: As a constructive, the move proposes a functional methodology for freedom centered on praise, blame, and incentives rather than a presupposed metaphysical essence.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The method is clear and productive, but the excerpt announces more of a research program than a completed analysis.

precisionFindings.rationale: The contrast between asking what freedom is and what it does is stable, with the relevant functions expressly enumerated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move presents room for a borrowed functional analysis rather than insisting that essence-based analysis is impossible.

charity.alternative: A metaphysical essence of freedom may be necessary to justify, rather than merely describe, praise and blame.
charity.decisiveQualification: Beginning from function does not itself prove that metaphysical questions are dispensable; it proposes an alternative order of analysis.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The methodological analogy is coherent, although successful functional explanation would not alone eliminate metaphysical residue.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Praise, blame, and incentives provide appropriate data for functional analysis, but the borrowed analogy is not fully defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally advances the compatibilist functional bridge, albeit less concretely than the deterministic-society example.

representationalCharity.rationale: The proposal leaves metaphysical supplementation open and does not caricature essence-based inquiry.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly adapts a what-it-does methodology and identifies proportional praise, blame, incentives, and disincentives as freedom's functions.

moves.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
moves.proposition: Even a deterministic society must retain a metaphysical distinction between agency and mere bodily occurrence because practical and moral life depend upon it.
moves.attributionBasis: A marked speaker transition begins the response, and Hawkins explicitly takes up the examples and functional claims from Folley's preceding turn.

components.text: Whether deterministic practical life can preserve a distinction between conduct attributable to an agent and mere bodily occurrence.
Whether analyzing freedom's functions is sufficient without a metaphysical account of genuine agency.
Whether incentive responsiveness alone supplies all distinctions needed for social coordination.

response.rationale: The reply accepts the practical distinction but argues that its lived and moral use presupposes metaphysical agency, directly challenging functional sufficiency.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive metaphysical-sufficiency issue but gives only a compressed argument for the presupposition.

precisionFindings.rationale: The agency-versus-spasm distinction is clear, though the content of the claimed metaphysical distinction remains underdefined.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim that denying free will makes social construction impossible exceeds the supplied argument because functional attribution could remain available.

charity.alternative: Compatibilists can distinguish intentional, reasons-responsive conduct from spasms without positing libertarian sourcehood.
charity.decisiveQualification: The persistence of a practical distinction does not establish that its metaphysical basis must be libertarian rather than functional or compatibilist.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The indispensability argument is intelligible, but it moves too quickly from practical attribution to a specifically metaphysical agency requirement.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The punch-versus-spasm example supports a distinction, not the stronger conclusion about its necessary metaphysical ground.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly advances the pro subsidiary-practice bridge by tying responsibility practices to real agency.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply accurately retains the compatibilist example but treats its required distinction as conceding more metaphysics than the example itself entails.

moves.evidenceBasis: The locked excerpt argues that a deterministic society still needs to distinguish punching someone from a muscle spasm and links that distinction to moral and practical agency.

moves.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
moves.proposition: Bradleyan idealism accepts scientific truths while rejecting the additional naturalist assumption that those truths exhaust everything real or experientially significant.
moves.attributionBasis: Folley explicitly invites Hawkins to explain Bradley, and the marked response is a long first-person exposition consistent with Hawkins's stated Bradleyan commitments.

response.rationale: As a constructive, the move accepts scientific explanation while isolating the additional exhaustiveness premise required for reductive naturalism.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It clearly advances the comparative idealist burden by separating scientific truth from the stronger 'nothing else' claim.

precisionFindings.rationale: Scientific truths, naturalistic exhaustiveness, and the Bradleyan acceptance-and-rejection structure are all plainly distinguished.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move does not reject science; it makes the bounded claim that exhaustiveness requires an additional assumption.

charity.alternative: Naturalism may treat scientific explanation as exhaustive because other truths supervene on or are integrated within scientific reality.
charity.decisiveQualification: The move challenges an added exhaustiveness premise without claiming that every naturalist simply denies experience or nonscientific discourse.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The separation of scientific claims from an exhaustiveness thesis is logically strong, though it does not itself prove additional ontological domains.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual burden-shift is well supported, but the positive evidence for unreduced truths is not developed in this span.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central idealism bridge by denying that scientific representation exhausts reality.

representationalCharity.rationale: The naturalist position is compressed, but the distinction between accepting science and disputing exhaustiveness remains fair.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt accepts truths produced by science while identifying 'there is nothing else' as an additional naturalistic assumption rejected by Bradleyan idealism.

moves.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
moves.proposition: Direct feeling and volitional agency precede intellectual systematization, so scientific representation is only one mode of access to reality.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage remains within Hawkins's extended answer and explicitly contrasts Bradley's view with Hegel's thought-centered idealism.

response.rationale: As a constructive, the move broadens access to reality beyond thought by identifying feeling and volitional agency as experientially prior dimensions.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It gives a clear Bradleyan integration claim, but the inference from experiential priority to ontological scope remains compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The contrast with thought-centered idealism is recoverable, though 'ground floor' and the priority of feeling permit epistemic and ontological readings.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The experiential observation supports multiple modes of engagement, but the claim that reality itself is therefore more than thought needs a bridge.

charity.alternative: Thought may systematically represent feeling and volition without implying that reality is reducible to occurrent abstract thought.
charity.decisiveQualification: Rejecting thought-only engagement does not by itself settle whether an intellectual system can integrate nonintellectual experience.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The route from feeling and agency to a non-thought-exhaustive reality is intelligible but requires an epistemic-to-ontological bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Direct experiential examples are relevant, yet they do not alone establish the full Bradleyan metaphysical conclusion.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move centrally supports integration of feeling, value-relevant agency, and thought beyond abstract rationalism.

representationalCharity.rationale: The contrast with Hegel is intelligible but somewhat compressed, leaving the strongest rationalist integration option underrepresented.

moves.evidenceBasis: The locked excerpt states that engagement with reality includes feeling, volition, and doing, and contrasts Bradley's view with the claim that the real is exhausted by the rational.

moves.speaker: Joe Folley
moves.proposition: A naturalistically acceptable idealism can treat experience as inquiry's subject matter and physical objects as constructed models without positing a mysterious mental substance.
moves.attributionBasis: A marked transition follows Hawkins addressing Joe, and the speaker's first-person Humean and Carnapian commitments identify the turn as Folley's.

components.text: Whether experience-centered inquiry requires Bradleyan metaphysics rather than a naturalistically acceptable idealism.
Whether feeling and agency as modes of access require reality to contain a mysterious mental substance.
Whether scientific models exhaust all legitimate truths about experience.

response.rationale: The reply offers a naturalistic idealism that centers experience and treats objects as models, contesting the alleged need for substantial mental reality without defending strict scientific exhaustiveness.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It provides a substantive rival framework and contacts the metaphysical-necessity issue while leaving some pro claims intact.

precisionFindings.rationale: The naturalistic phenomenalist direction is recoverable, though 'idealism,' 'constructed models,' and 'mental stuff' remain somewhat conversationally unstable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker offers the position as a naturalistically acceptable possibility and avoids claiming a completed reduction.

charity.alternative: Bradleyan idealism need not posit a separable mysterious mental substance; it may claim systematic experiential integration.
charity.decisiveQualification: Refuting a crude mental-stuff ontology does not by itself remove the pro claim that experience includes irreducible value, feeling, and agency.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The path from experience as subject matter to physical objects as constructed models is coherent, with details of construction left open.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Phenomenalist and model-based considerations support the possibility, but its explanatory constraints are not fully supplied.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally advances disciplined experience-centered inquiry without commitment to a substantial absolute.

representationalCharity.rationale: The alternative is constructive and serious, but its contrast partly relies on a weaker mental-substance rendering of the idealist position.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt distinguishes a naturalistically acceptable, experience-centered idealism from claims about mysterious mental stuff and treats inquiry as making sense of experience.

moves.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
moves.proposition: Although reflective subjects cannot recover wholly precognitive experience, unbounded feeling is ultimately integrated with complete structure, value, and agency in the absolute.
moves.attributionBasis: Hawkins explicitly turns to Folley's remaining question and gives a continuous Bradleyan answer until Folley introduces a comparison with Peirce.

components.text: Whether a naturalistically acceptable experience-centered idealism can avoid Bradley's substantially integrated absolute.
Whether treating physical objects as constructed models supplies adequate disciplined inquiry.

response.rationale: The move develops Bradley's positive absolute and its integration of feeling, structure, value, and agency, but it does not directly test the naturalistic rival's adequacy.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It supplies highly relevant contrary metaphysics without component-level engagement with the earlier naturalistic proposal.

precisionFindings.rationale: The integrative claim is recoverable, but 'at the end of all time,' attainability, and the status of the absolute are not fully stabilized.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim that all experience, structure, value, and agency must unite in the absolute substantially exceeds the warrant presented in the excerpt.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The synthesis is intelligible, but the necessity of ultimate unity and its relation to temporal completion require major bridges.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move describes Bradley's system but provides limited independent support for the absolute's existence or necessary integration.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central absolute bridge by specifying the integration of feeling, structure, value, and agency.

representationalCharity.rationale: The span primarily states the positive Bradleyan account and does not materially reconstruct an opposing interpretation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt states that every consciousness and feeling unites with complete structure and moral-volitional history in the absolute, where truth, goodness, and beauty are attained.

moves.speaker: Joe Folley
moves.proposition: The Bradleyan absolute may function only as a regulative ideal of completed inquiry, leaving its substantial existence or attainability unsettled.
moves.attributionBasis: Folley explicitly frames the comparison with C. S. Peirce, contrasts possible interpretations, and asks how certain Bradley is about the absolute's existence.

components.text: Whether the absolute substantially exists or is only a regulative ideal of completed inquiry.
Whether finite reflective subjects can attain or verify the proposed completed integration.

response.rationale: The Peircean comparison directly presses both ontological existence and attainability, exposing that the pro description alone does not settle either status.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It targets the decisive existence-versus-regulative-ideal ambiguity and explicitly asks about the residual agnosticism.

precisionFindings.rationale: Regulative ideal, substantial existence, possible attainability, and Bradley's degree of agnosticism are clearly distinguished.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move appropriately frames the comparison as an unresolved question rather than presuming that Bradley's absolute is merely regulative.

charity.alternative: Bradley may affirm the absolute as real and not merely as an indefinitely approached theory.
charity.decisiveQualification: Affirmation of existence still requires a warrant distinguishing ontological reality from inquiry's regulative orientation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between a regulative endpoint and an existent completed reality is precise and exposes a genuine evidential gap.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The Peircean analogy is apt diagnostic support, though analogy alone does not determine Bradley's actual commitment.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central absolute bridge at the existence and completion claims required by the route.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply expressly presents both substantial and regulative readings and asks how strongly Bradley commits to the former.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts an existent absolute that may or may not be reached with Peircean end-of-inquiry truth and explicitly asks how agnostic Bradley is.

moves.speaker: Nathan Hawkins
moves.proposition: The absolute is not merely a settled theory because inquiry's normative orientation toward completion recognizes a reality fuller than present partial understanding.
moves.attributionBasis: The pro speaker labels Folley's question, states Bradley's lack of agnosticism, and gives reasons before Folley begins a practical analogy.

components.text: Whether the absolute is merely a regulative ideal rather than a reality fuller than present partial understanding.
What warrants the substantial existence or attainability of the absolute beyond inquiry's normative orientation.

response.rationale: The reply denies the merely regulative reading and invokes the normative direction of truth, beauty, feeling, and goodness, but it does not fully bridge orientation to existence.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive interpretive alternative yet leaves the central ontological warrant substantially unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The normative-orientation argument is recoverable, though 'more real' shifts between completeness, normativity, and ontological status.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Recognizing inquiry's aim at completeness does not by itself warrant the necessary existence or superior reality of a completed whole.

charity.alternative: Inquiry can be normatively oriented toward an ideal completion without that completion substantially existing or ever being attainable.
charity.decisiveQualification: Normative direction establishes a standard of inquiry more readily than an ontological entity that already possesses completion.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from aiming at completion to recognizing a more-real completed whole contains a major modal and ontological bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Normative practices support an ideal of completion, but they weakly support the stronger existence claim.
